statement

In the Swedish cohort, men who reported using cannabis more than 50 times at conscription had a hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for lung cancer against men who reported never using it, adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription; the committee says studies in an epidemiologic review that are not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk. No absolute risks are given in the committee's account.

In the Swedish cohort (the paper itself), 'heavy' use meant reporting, once, at conscription at age 18 to 20, more than 50 uses of cannabis in a lifetime (831 men, 1.7%). These men had a hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for lung cancer against men who reported never using cannabis, adjusted for tobacco smoking (in three bands: none, 1 to 10 and more than 10 cigarettes a day), alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status, each measured only at conscription; unadjusted it was 3.72 (1.96–7.06), and adjusted for tobacco alone 2.24 (1.17–4.29). Ever having used cannabis was not associated with lung cancer once tobacco was counted (1.25, 0.84–1.87, from 1.90 unadjusted), and the lower bands of use showed no rise with more use (fully adjusted, from once to 11 to 50 uses: 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68, none significant); the authors report no clear dose–response relationship. Of the men in the heaviest band, 91% also smoked tobacco (62% more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 23% of the men who never used cannabis), and analyses within tobacco groups were unstable or could not be estimated because too few men used cannabis without tobacco. Over follow-up from 1970 to 2009 (about 1.9 million person-years), 189 of the 49,321 men had a lung cancer record (about 4 in 1,000; 179 in the analyses); the paper gives no count by cannabis group, so absolute risks by group cannot be given. The committee says studies in an epidemiologic review that are not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk.
statement
in the cohort, cannabis and tobacco use after conscription were not followed, its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis, and the self-reports were not anonymous.

in the cohort (confirmed in its paper), cannabis and tobacco use after conscription were not recorded, nor how cannabis was smoked, how much or how strong it was; its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco into their cannabis, which they say would inflate the cannabis-related risk; and the self-reports were not anonymous, which they say may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have over-reported to be exempted from military training. Follow-up ended when the men were 58 to 60 (editors' calculation from birth years 1949 to 1951), younger than the median age of about 70 at a first lung cancer diagnosis that the authors cite; lung cancers came from hospital inpatient records to 2009 and death records to 2006, not from the cancer register; and the 7.6% of men who did not answer the cannabis questions had a lower risk than men who reported never using it (0.41, 0.17–0.99).

the cohort paper was funded by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and by the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research, which the paper says had no role in the study, and its authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the pooled analysis is not given in the committee's account and is not known here.
plain

A long study of Swedish men found about twice the rate of lung cancer in men who had said, when called up for military service, that they had used cannabis more than 50 times, but it did not follow what they smoked later in life.

A long study of Swedish men found about twice the rate of lung cancer in men who had said, when called up for military service at 18 to 20, that they had used cannabis more than 50 times, compared with men who said they never had, even after taking into account the tobacco they smoked then. But nearly all of those men also smoked tobacco, men who had used cannabis fewer times showed no clear rise, nobody recorded what anyone smoked later in life, and the study ended when the men were about 60, younger than the age at which lung cancer is usually found.

Swedish conscript cohort (the paper; 1970 to 2009, about 1.9 million person-years; 179 lung cancers among 44,257 in the frequency analysis): more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) fully adjusted (tobacco in three bands, alcohol, respiratory conditions, socioeconomic status, all at conscription); tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17–4.29); crude 3.72 (1.96–7.06). Fully adjusted, lower bands: once 1.52 (0.77–3.01); 2 to 4 times 0.66 (0.27–1.62); 5 to 10 times 0.68 (0.21–2.16); 11 to 50 times 1.68 (0.77–3.66). Ever against never: crude 1.90 (1.30–2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85–1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco, more than 10 cigarettes a day against none: 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Absolute: 189 lung cancers among 49,321 men by the end of 2009 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000; editors' calculation); no counts by cannabis group.

set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Pooled analysis: not appraisable here, seen only through the committee's account (a narrative review; METHODS §6.3), with self-reported exposure without biological confirmation and no account of smoking technique or of the cannabis smoked. Swedish cohort, now read in full (card sc_callaghan_2013): ROBINS-E high, for confounding (tobacco measured once, at age 18 to 20, in three bands, with 91% of the heaviest cannabis band also smoking tobacco; the ever-use association disappeared with this adjustment, so residual confounding by tobacco amount and by later smoking is plausible and would run away from the null) and for exposure measurement (one non-anonymous report of lifetime use 40 years before the outcome; no record of use after conscription, of how cannabis was smoked or of tobacco mixed in).
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Second-hand reading of the pooled analysis; exposure definitions differ between the two sources (at least 1 joint-year; more than 50 lifetime uses by age 18 to 20); the cohort is of Swedish men followed only to about age 60, with use as it was in 1969–70; the outcome is incidence of lung cancer with self-reported past use.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The pooled interval (0.66–1.38) and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, 0.51–2.08 include no difference and a rise; the adenocarcinoma intervals (0.75–4.00; 0.85–3.56) are wide; few people with heavy long-term smoking; in the cohort the heaviest band (831 men) gives 1.08–4.14, and too few men used cannabis without tobacco for any estimate in that group.
set.grade.domains.dose_response.note: Not counted: in the pooled analysis risk rose with duration and intensity, not significantly; in the cohort the bands below more than 50 uses showed no gradient (fully adjusted 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68) and the authors report no clear dose–response relationship.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational (case-control studies and one cohort), so the claim starts low. It rests on the National Academies committee's account of the pooled case-control analysis (a narrative review; the pooled analysis was not read, so its figures are second-hand and its risk of bias cannot be appraised, METHODS §6.3) and on the Swedish cohort's own paper, read in full (ROBINS-E high). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 pass the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two would give the same. The relation is insufficient evidence (METHODS §6.1): neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision, because the pooled interval does not exclude a rise of 38% (and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, an odds ratio of 2.08), while the cohort's raised estimate is confined to its heaviest band, with no gradient below it, no association for ever use once tobacco was counted, tobacco smoked by 91% of that band and no estimate possible for men who did not smoke tobacco. The committee's grade, moderate evidence of no statistical association, is its own judgment and concerns statistical significance; the editors do not adopt it as a finding of no effect (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs precision). Not rated as 'causes': every source is observational and none can show cause. The status is mixed (a pooled null and a cohort that points up in one band, not reconciled by the committee; the cohort paper does not resolve it). With the cohort paper read, the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; it stays a draft as a section 7 claim held for the senior author.
set.verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on the National Academies report (Chapter 5 lung cancer section, Chapter 5 gaps and summary, Appendix B; read in full text on NCBI Bookshelf), the Cousijn commentary and, from batch 10, the Swedish conscript cohort's own paper (Callaghan et al., 2013), read in full by AI reader 91 (first reader) from the online-first PDF, which has no printed page numbers, so its anchors cite the PDF's pages 1 to 10 (the electronic supplement with the tobacco-stratified tables was not available). The cohort's exposure definition, adjustment, crude and tobacco-adjusted estimates, the null ever-use result, the absence of a gradient, tobacco co-use, follow-up to about age 60, outcome sources and funding now come from the paper; the eight new anchors need a second reader. The committee anchor that describes the cohort (evidence 1) still says the cohort paper was not read, which is now out of date. Not read and without a reference record: Zhang et al. 2015, the pooled analysis (DOI 10.1002/ijc.29036) and Huang et al. 2015, the epidemiologic review (DOI 10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-14-1026). The relation insufficient-evidence and the certainty very low are the editors' reading under METHODS §6.1 and §6.3, not the committee's: its grade concerns statistical significance over a pooled interval that does not exclude a rise, with a cohort pointing up in its heaviest band, and its chapter highlight is stronger than its numbered conclusion. The cohort's full text does not settle the question, so mixed is kept; the senior author may still prefer contested, with a debate box. Cousijn's table drops the word statistical from the committee's cancer conclusion, and its criticism of a 500-participant cut-off was not found in the chapters read, so the commentary is used only for the tobacco co-use point and the WHO contrast (the WHO report was not read). Head and neck cancer (Conclusion 5-2) was read and is on the study card, not in this claim. No industry sponsor of the report is listed; the cohort was funded by an Ontario ministry grant to CAMH and a Swedish research council, with no conflicts declared; the funding of the pooled analysis is not known here. The simple line gives no amounts.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results); Materials and methods › Swedish male conscripts' files; Measurement of cannabis use
evidence_add.extracted: Cohort and exposure: 49,321 men aged 18 to 20 conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–1970 (more than 97% of Swedish men of that age; 2–3% were excused for disqualifying conditions), linked to the Patient Register, the National Cause-of-Death Register and the Total Population Register. Cannabis use was self-reported once, at conscription, in a non-anonymous questionnaire: ever against never, and lifetime frequency (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times); this paper calls more than 50 times heavy use. At baseline 10.5% (5,156) reported lifetime use and 1.7% (831) more than 50 uses.

evidence_add.locator: Materials and methods › Measurement of tobacco use; Potential confounders; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (never and more-than-50 columns)
evidence_add.extracted: Tobacco and other covariates: tobacco was measured once, at conscription, as cigarettes smoked a day (none 41.4%, 1–5 a day 11.2%, 6–10 20.7%, 11–20 23.1%, more than 20 3.6%), collapsed into three bands for the models: none, 1–10 and more than 10 a day. Of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 60 (7.2%) did not smoke tobacco, 242 (29.1%) smoked 1–10 a day, 514 (61.8%) more than 10 and 15 (1.8%) gave no tobacco answer; of the 40,397 men reporting never using cannabis, 18,100 (44.8%) did not smoke tobacco, 12,725 (31.5%) smoked 1–10 a day and 9,364 (23.2%) more than 10. Alcohol above 250 g a week: 23.1% against 2.3%. Respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) about 2% in each group; socioeconomic status from occupation in the 1970 census. The Results say about 91% of the heaviest band reported some tobacco use.

evidence_add.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (more than 50 times row; footnotes a and b)
evidence_add.extracted: More than 50 lifetime uses at conscription against never, Cox regression on 44,257 men with 179 lung cancers: hazard ratio 3.72 (95% CI 1.96 to 7.06) crude, 2.24 (1.17 to 4.29) adjusted for tobacco in three bands, and 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14) fully adjusted for tobacco, alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions at conscription and socioeconomic status in 1970. The authors describe it as more than a twofold risk even after these adjustments.

evidence_add.locator: Results, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Table 3; Table 4 (once to 11–50 times rows); Table 2
evidence_add.extracted: No association for any use once tobacco was counted, and no gradient below the heaviest band: ever against never, crude 1.90 (1.30 to 2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85 to 1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84 to 1.87), on 44,285 men with 179 cancers, the authors saying tobacco adjustment greatly attenuated the risk. Lifetime frequency, fully adjusted against never: once 1.52 (0.77 to 3.01), 2–4 times 0.66 (0.27 to 1.62), 5–10 times 0.68 (0.21 to 2.16), 11–50 times 1.68 (0.77 to 3.66); crude, once 2.07 (1.06 to 4.06) and 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26 to 5.74). The authors state that the results did not show a clear dose–response relationship. Tobacco in the same models showed a strong gradient: fully adjusted 2.34 (1.47 to 3.70) for 1–10 and 5.03 (3.23 to 7.81) for more than 10 cigarettes a day against none.

evidence_add.locator: Materials and methods › Study outcome; Validity of lung cancer outcome codes; Statistical analyses; Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: Follow-up and outcome: from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men) to lung cancer, death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009, about 1.9 million person-years in each analysis. Lung cancer (ICD-8/9 162; ICD-10 C33–C34) came from the Patient Register (inpatient care, any diagnostic position) to the end of 2009 and from the Cause-of-Death Register (underlying cause) to the end of 2006; the authors cite 78% to 99% concordance between registers. 189 men had incident lung cancer (95 in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only, 6 in the death register only), 2,958 (6.0%) died of other causes and 930 (1.9%) emigrated; ten cancers were excluded for missing predictors. Cancers by cannabis group are shown only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year (values not extracted), so no absolute risk by group can be given. The authors note that the only earlier cohort ended at a mean age of 42 and that the median age at a first lung cancer diagnosis is about 70. Editors' calculation: men born in 1949 to 1951 were 58 to 60 at the end of follow-up, and 189 of 49,321 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) had a lung cancer record by then.

evidence_add.locator: Materials and methods › Missing data; Results, 5th paragraph and its continuation after Table 4
evidence_add.extracted: Missing answers: cannabis answers were missing for 3,768 men (7.64%; ever use) and 3,800 (7.70%; frequency). Against men reporting never using cannabis, these men were not more likely to develop lung cancer: ever-use item crude 0.52 (0.24 to 1.10), tobacco-adjusted 0.47 (0.21 to 1.07), fully adjusted 0.41 (0.17 to 0.99); frequency item 0.51 (0.24 to 1.09), 0.47 (0.21 to 1.06) and 0.40 (0.16 to 0.98). The authors ran these models to check whether the men who did not answer had used cannabis heavily; the paper does not explain their lower risk.

evidence_add.locator: Results, last paragraph (Supplemental Tables 1–2); Discussion, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Conclusions
evidence_add.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on cannabis or tobacco use before conscription and none after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the heavy group reported some tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting of cannabis use, while anecdotal information suggests some men inflated their use to be exempted from military training. Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) gave unstable or inestimable results, because most people who used cannabis, especially frequently, also used tobacco and lung cancer was uncommon. The authors argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null. Their conclusion calls the finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise lung cancer risk, and the Discussion proposes its use in drug-prevention programmes. Editors' note: later tobacco smoking, if more common in the men who used cannabis, would bias the estimate away from the null; the paper covers this only as residual confounding by tobacco.

evidence_add.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflict of interest
evidence_add.extracted: Funding as printed: supported indirectly by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, which helped provide salary support for the first author, and by a research grant from the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research (FAS 2009-1611) that helped provide salary support for the third author; the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, manuscript preparation or approval to publish. The authors declare no conflict of interest.

The systematic review and the committee draw on some of the same cohorts (CARDIA, Dunedin, Los Angeles), so they are not independent confirmations of each other; a 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route of use (42 sources, 15 of them empirical studies; nothing pooled or appraised, and its search string excluded the term tobacco) adds no independent cohort, since its lung studies are CARDIA, Dunedin, Los Angeles, NHANES and Vancouver, and is used here only for its comparisons of routes and the figures it relays.
statement
The review rated its own evidence for cough, phlegm and wheeze 'low'.

The review rated its own evidence for cough, phlegm and wheeze 'low'. In NHANES (US adults, 2007 to 2010, cross-sectional; the 2024 review's account, percentages not adjusted), cough, cold, phlegm or a respiratory illness in the past week was reported by 16.9% of people who had not smoked cannabis in the past 30 days against 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of those who smoked it on 1 to 5, 6 to 20 and more than 20 days, and wheeze in the past year by 12.4% against 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5%.
statement
Whether tobacco was mixed into joints was not recorded in CARDIA or the Ontario data.

Whether tobacco was mixed into joints was not recorded in CARDIA or the Ontario data. In a Vancouver sample of 878 adults aged 40 or more (the 2024 review's account; the comparison group is not named there), people who had smoked at least 50 joints and no tobacco were not at significantly greater risk of COPD or breathing symptoms, while people who had smoked both had higher odds of COPD (2.90, 1.53–5.51) and of symptoms (2.39, 1.58–3.62).
statement

The only comparison with another way of taking cannabis in the parts read is a 12-person study without a control group, in which symptoms resolved about a month after people switched from smoking to a vaporizer (the committee's account); the committee lists whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms as unknown.

Comparisons with other ways of taking cannabis are few, small and second-hand. The vaporizer study without a control group enrolled 22 people who used cannabis often and had breathing symptoms; after a month, the 12 who had not developed a respiratory illness reported fewer symptoms and had a higher FVC, while FEV1 did not change significantly (the 2024 review's account; the committee described a 12-person study in which symptoms resolved). In a laboratory crossover (11 people who smoked cannabis often and 9 occasionally), smoked cannabis raised exhaled carbon monoxide more than vaporised cannabis, and breathing rate did not change with either; in another laboratory study blunts gave more carbon monoxide than joints; and Canadian medical cannabis patients (a survey of 364) rated vaporizing and eating as less harmful to breathing than smoking. The committee lists whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms as unknown, and the 2024 review calls its conclusions by route tentative.

the committee's report, US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed; the 2024 review by route, no funding and no conflicts declared.
plain
The only comparison with another way of taking cannabis was one small study of 12 people with no comparison group, in which symptoms eased about a month after a switch from smoking to a vaporizer.

Comparisons with other ways of taking cannabis are few and small: in a study with no comparison group, breathing symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, among the people who did not catch a chest illness during that month; in a laboratory study, smoking put more carbon monoxide into the breath than vaporizing; and medical cannabis patients rated vaporizing and eating as easier on their breathing than smoking.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract; Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note; Study selection, abstraction, and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
evidence_add.extracted: The 2024 review by route: a systematic review without meta-analysis, guided by PRISMA, with no protocol or registration stated. Search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed English-language articles from January 2009 to December 2023 reporting the route of administration, with cannabis confirmed by drug screening; studies including other illicit drugs, or people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions, excluded. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco. 1,873 records, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis of tweets, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Abstract selection was independent (kappa 0.89). The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grades and no appraisal of individual studies are reported, and nothing was pooled.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Empirical studies › Respiratory effects, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Kempker 2015, Tan 2009, Hancox 2010, Tashkin 2012, Fiorelli 2013 rows)
evidence_add.extracted: Smoking and breathing, single studies as the review relays them: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (Kempker 2015; US adults, cross-sectional): cough, cold, phlegm or respiratory illness in the past 7 days in 16.9%, 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of people who smoked cannabis on 0, 1–5, 6–20 and more than 20 of the past 30 days, and wheeze in the past year in 12.4%, 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5% (as printed, unadjusted); more than 20 joint-years against no exposure, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (95% CI 1.1 to 3.9), with no association at lower cumulative exposure. Vancouver (Tan 2009; random sample of 878 people aged 40 or more, spirometry): people who had smoked at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco were not at significantly greater risk of COPD or respiratory symptoms; people who had smoked both had higher odds of COPD (OR 2.90, 1.53 to 5.51) and of symptoms (OR 2.39, 1.58 to 3.62), adjusted for age, asthma and comorbidities; the review does not name the comparison group, and its text calls this smoking cannabis in a joint combined with tobacco while its Table 4 describes people who smoked both. Dunedin (Hancox 2010; 1,037 people followed to age 32): cumulative use associated with higher FVC, lung volumes and airway resistance but not with FEV1, the FEV1/FVC ratio or gas transfer. Los Angeles (Tashkin 2012; 299 people followed 9.8 years): more chronic bronchitis at follow-up with continued cannabis smoking than in never or former smokers. Naples (Fiorelli 2013; people treated for spontaneous pneumothorax, 13 who smoked cannabis and 140 who did not, 135 of them tobacco smokers): bullae in 8 (62%) against 110 (78%) overall and, under age 35, in 7 of 10 against 3 of 10, though the text says cannabis smoking predisposed to bullous lung disease.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Empirical studies › Cardiovascular effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Respiratory effects, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Cooper and Haney 2009, Newmeyer 2017 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Second
evidence_add.extracted: Routes compared in the same people (laboratory studies, second-hand): Newmeyer 2017 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally; smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis in separate sessions): smoking produced significantly greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h after dosing; route had no significant effect on breathing rate or blood pressure; heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, increases that did not differ significantly between routes. Cooper and Haney 2009 (24 healthy volunteers; blunts against joints of the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent. The review's Discussion gives the Newmeyer sample as n = 11, against 11 and 9 in its Table 4.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Literature reviews, 3rd paragraph; Table 3 (Russell 2017 row); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 2nd paragraph; Table 4 (Newmeyer 2017, Shiplo 2016, Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Nevertheless
evidence_add.extracted: Vaping in the review (second-hand): three empirical studies have a vaping arm, and all compare vaping with smoking, not with no use. Newmeyer 2017 (the laboratory crossover; dried cannabis in a vaporizer). Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post design, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness during the trial had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007 as printed), while FEV1 did not change significantly (p = 0.053 as printed); the amount used a day fell slightly and not significantly (p = 0.10 as printed), though the text says vaping reduced it. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape over time, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. Editors' calculation: two-tailed p values for t(11) = 2.90 and 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 are about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so the printed values match one-tailed tests, and the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs beginning Nevertheless, First, Second and Third; Strength and limitations; Conclusion; Disclosure statement; Funding
evidence_add.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled or appraised (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

No other study of cannabis vaping and breathing symptoms or lung function was read for this batch, and the authors say longitudinal research is lacking.

A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled or appraised; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this survey is not among its sources) found no study comparing people who vape cannabis with people who do not use it, and none following people who vape over time. Its vaping evidence, second-hand, compares vaping with smoking: in a laboratory crossover (11 adults who smoked cannabis often and 9 occasionally; dried cannabis in a vaporizer), vaporised cannabis raised exhaled carbon monoxide less than smoked cannabis and breathing rate did not change with either; Canadian medical cannabis patients (a survey of 364) rated vaporizing as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and in a one-month study without a control group, 22 people who used cannabis often and had breathing symptoms switched to a vaporizer, and the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness reported fewer symptoms and had a higher FVC, with FEV1 not significantly changed. None of these studied THC oil cartridges or dabs, and the survey's authors say longitudinal research is lacking.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract; Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note; Study selection, abstraction, and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
evidence_add.extracted: The 2024 review by route: a systematic review without meta-analysis, guided by PRISMA, with no protocol or registration stated. Search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed English-language articles from January 2009 to December 2023 reporting the route of administration, with cannabis confirmed by drug screening; studies including other illicit drugs, or people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions, excluded. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco. 1,873 records, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis of tweets, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Abstract selection was independent (kappa 0.89). The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grades and no appraisal of individual studies are reported, and nothing was pooled.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Empirical studies › Cardiovascular effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Respiratory effects, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Cooper and Haney 2009, Newmeyer 2017 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Second
evidence_add.extracted: Routes compared in the same people (laboratory studies, second-hand): Newmeyer 2017 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally; smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis in separate sessions): smoking produced significantly greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h after dosing; route had no significant effect on breathing rate or blood pressure; heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, increases that did not differ significantly between routes. Cooper and Haney 2009 (24 healthy volunteers; blunts against joints of the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent. The review's Discussion gives the Newmeyer sample as n = 11, against 11 and 9 in its Table 4.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Literature reviews, 3rd paragraph; Table 3 (Russell 2017 row); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 2nd paragraph; Table 4 (Newmeyer 2017, Shiplo 2016, Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Nevertheless
evidence_add.extracted: Vaping in the review (second-hand): three empirical studies have a vaping arm, and all compare vaping with smoking, not with no use. Newmeyer 2017 (the laboratory crossover; dried cannabis in a vaporizer). Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post design, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness during the trial had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007 as printed), while FEV1 did not change significantly (p = 0.053 as printed); the amount used a day fell slightly and not significantly (p = 0.10 as printed), though the text says vaping reduced it. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape over time, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. Editors' calculation: two-tailed p values for t(11) = 2.90 and 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 are about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so the printed values match one-tailed tests, and the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups.

The overview also infers that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, citing no study of people who eat cannabis, and nothing read here compares the lungs of people who eat cannabis with those who smoke it.

The overview also infers that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, citing no study of people who eat cannabis. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled or appraised; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this hospital study is not among its sources) also found no study of the lungs of adults who eat cannabis. Its oral-route evidence, second-hand, is a laboratory crossover in which heart rate rose about as much after eating cannabis as after smoking or vaporising it (about 10 to 13 beats a minute above placebo) and breathing rate did not change with route; a survey in which Canadian medical cannabis patients rated eating as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and records of children who ate cannabis products (calls to US poison centres and two hospital chart reviews), in which a fast heart rate was common, some children needed help with breathing, and severe heart and breathing effects were seen at higher doses for their body weight. Its abstract nonetheless says edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Cardiovascular effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 4 (Cao 2016, Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016 rows); Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: Oral route in the review (second-hand): five empirical studies have an oral arm. In adults, the Newmeyer 2017 laboratory crossover found heart rate 13.0 and 10.2 beats a minute above placebo at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, not significantly different from smoked or vaporised cannabis, and no effect of route on blood pressure or breathing rate; in the Shiplo 2016 survey of 364 Canadian medical cannabis patients, eating was rated lower in perceived respiratory harm than smoking. The other three are records of exposures, mostly in young children: Cao 2016 (430 exposures to cannabis food products reported to US poison centres, 2013 to 2015): tachycardia in 84 (printed as 31%, which 430 cannot give), chest pain or hypotension in a few, and respiratory depression in 3, reported only in children aged 5 or younger; Kaczor 2021 (chart review of 32 children): 5 (16%) needed respiratory support; Pepin 2023 (records of 80 children younger than 6 with a known THC dose): tachycardia and hypotension most common, with severe cardiovascular toxicity and severe respiratory symptoms (hypoxia, then apnea and bradypnea) at recorded doses above 2 mg/kg of body weight. The Abstract nonetheless says cannabis edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects, and the Discussion that severe cardiovascular effects were associated with higher THC doses in all routes. No included study measured lung function or breathing symptoms in adults who eat cannabis against adults who do not use it.
